samples.reason: Voice calibration only — must-be-true item. Shares the passage-oriented stem voice ('properly inferred from the passage') but asks for what FOLLOWS from the text rather than what the AUTHOR'S main conclusion is.

question.difficultyReason: Dense historical stimulus with multiple events. Traps (A) and (D) overreach what the passage says; (C) introduces information about analytical capability that the passage does not establish.
question.stimulus: During the construction of the Quebec Bridge in 1907, the bridge's designer, Theodore Cooper, received word that the suspended span being built out from the bridge's cantilever was deflecting downward by a fraction of an inch (2.54 centimeters). Before he could telegraph to freeze the project, the whole cantilever arm broke off and plunged, along with seven dozen workers, into the St. Lawrence River. It was the worst bridge construction disaster in history. As a direct result of the inquiry that followed, the engineering 'rules of thumb' by which thousands of bridges had been built around the world went down with the Quebec Bridge. Twentieth-century bridge engineers would thereafter depend on far more rigorous applications of mathematical analysis.
question.questionStem: Which one of the following statements can be properly inferred from the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bridges built before about 1907 were built without thorough mathematical analysis and, therefore, were unsafe for the public to use.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cooper's absence from the Quebec Bridge construction site resulted in the breaking off of the cantilever.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Nineteenth-century bridge engineers relied on their rules of thumb because analytical methods were inadequate to solve their design problems.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Only a more rigorous application of mathematical analysis to the design of the Quebec Bridge could have prevented its collapse.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Prior to 1907 the mathematical analysis incorporated in engineering rules of thumb was insufficient to completely assure the safety of bridges under construction.

explanations.correct: The passage explicitly says the rules of thumb that had built thousands of bridges went down with the Quebec Bridge, and engineers thereafter adopted more rigorous analysis. From this you can infer those prior rules were not sufficient to fully assure safety.
explanations.A: Too strong — the passage doesn't say bridges were broadly unsafe for public use.
explanations.B: Cooper's location isn't discussed as causal.
explanations.C: The passage doesn't say analytical methods were inadequate; it says engineers relied on rules of thumb.
explanations.D: Too strong — 'only' a rigorous analysis rules out other possible preventions.

source.notes: Verbatim from LSAC public LR sample page. Correct answer E confirmed.

samples.reason: Voice calibration only — principle-justify item. Multi-claim LR stimulus useful for modeling the conclusion-with-support structure main-point items rely on.

question.difficultyReason: Requires selecting the principle that most directly licenses the specific claim about middle-class members of poor nations. Trap (D) makes a sweeping claim that superficially matches.
question.stimulus: Journalist: To reconcile the need for profits sufficient to support new drug research with the moral imperative to provide medicines to those who most need them but cannot afford them, some pharmaceutical companies feel justified in selling a drug in rich nations at one price and in poor nations at a much lower price. But this practice is unjustified. A nation with a low average income may still have a substantial middle class better able to pay for new drugs than are many of the poorer citizens of an overall wealthier nation.
question.questionStem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the journalist's reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: People who are ill deserve more consideration than do healthy people, regardless of their relative socioeconomic positions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Wealthy institutions have an obligation to expend at least some of their resources to assist those incapable of assisting themselves.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Whether one deserves special consideration depends on one's needs rather than on characteristics of the society to which one belongs.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The people in wealthy nations should not have better access to health care than do the people in poorer nations.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Unequal access to health care is more unfair than an unequal distribution of wealth.

explanations.correct: The journalist's complaint is that pricing by nation ignores the fact that individual ability-to-pay varies within and across nations. Principle C — deserving consideration depends on individual needs, not society-level characteristics — directly underwrites that critique.
explanations.A: Concerns illness vs. health, not rich-nation vs. poor-nation.
explanations.B: Institutional obligation is not the journalist's subject.
explanations.D: Inverts the journalist's point — the journalist isn't arguing for equal access but against nation-level pricing.
explanations.E: Comparative fairness is not what the journalist is defending.

source.notes: Verbatim from LSAC public LR sample page. Correct answer C confirmed.
